name: Emeka Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day like at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and only recently started answering calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school, but I'm still learning the billing rules and sometimes need the trainer to take over. I like the caller who says thank you when a charge finally makes sense. I don't use the AI answer box.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you carry home from a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly worry about whether I kept up. My wife works part-time in a school kitchen, our two children are still in school, and the mortgage takes both our wages. I'm on the lower pay here, with less than a month's expenses saved. There aren't many other centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the phone still needs someone to answer it properly. A quicker form won't settle a caller who cannot understand a charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm glad there is no large change, but I still lie awake over the mortgage. I'm 43 and new to this centre; my pay is low, and we have less than a month's bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the calls assigned to me and ask the trainer to check the ones I get wrong. Starting now, my wife and I will drop the paid television package and put that money toward the mortgage buffer through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, calmer about the job. One missed paycheque could put us behind on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your wife's income fit the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife works part-time at a school kitchen, and we need both wages for the mortgage. Her hours change by term, so I cannot count that money twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the answer box yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't used the AI answer box. I would rather ask the trainer when a billing rule is unclear than guess from a machine.

do: Keep taking **assigned calls** and get trainer feedback.
Put the freed money into a **mortgage buffer** through the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about mortgage money, though work feels steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to ask which shifts will go when the software starts answering people. I don't want the junior desk to vanish behind a new dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would be one of the first names removed if easy calls disappear. I'm still learning this job, and there are few other centres near our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask my supervisor for a written shift plan and keep practising the difficult billing rules with the trainer. If my hours fall in the first year, I'll stop our weekend takeaway and ask the hardware shop near my church about a posted paid counter vacancy before leaving the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The mortgage doesn't get smaller because a program can answer faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I would tell the children we are eating at home more often, not make them carry the job worry. We'd check the mortgage payment before buying anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the shop job possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the shop to offer regular paid hours and enough take-home pay for the mortgage. A promise that I might become permanent after unpaid work is no use to us.

I'd want a **written plan** before the centre changes its queue.

Practise **billing rules** with the trainer during paid shifts.

feel: **Alarmed** because lost hours would threaten the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need actual dismissal dates if general AI can answer the calls by 2028. Robots around 2031 don't give my headset job three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the centre could cut me before I have mastered the job. My wife's kitchen wage won't cover the mortgage and two schoolchildren by itself, and our reserve is under one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll gather our mortgage papers and ask the centre for its written notice terms. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for advertised paid shop-counter jobs nearby and ask my brother for a short loan only if the mortgage payment is due before another wage arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and tired just picturing it. I have things to ask, but almost no money for a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who hears the news at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my wife before the children heard rumours from me. We would work out which payment has to be covered first, then explain only the change in our routine to the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could your brother actually help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother might lend us one mortgage payment, but I would ask whether he can spare it and agree when I could repay him. I cannot treat family as an endless bank.

I'd say **2031 robots** do not delay our 2028 telephone risk.
think: I expect my **junior job** could end before I master it.
I know my wife's **kitchen wage** cannot cover the household mortgage alone.
do: Gather **mortgage papers** and request written notice tomorrow.
Apply for **advertised paid counter jobs** after an actual job loss.

fieldNote: His **household arithmetic** drives the fear more than a dislike of technology.

steps.text: Apply for advertised paid shop-counter jobs if his centre post ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years gives us time to learn which paid jobs are left. It still puts general AI on the phones in 2031, before robots doing hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might get good enough at hard calls to stay a bit longer, but I cannot bank the house on that. Five years would let us add to savings and see whether the hardware shop needs a trained counter worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask my supervisor for more supervised complaint calls on paid shifts and put any extra hours into the mortgage buffer. Before 2031, if the hardware shop posts a paid opening with steady hours, I'll apply; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep my centre job if it still pays and otherwise take a suitable written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe more easily than in the two-year picture. I can practise without quitting the job we need now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would supervised practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the trainer to sit with me on one disputed bill each week. I can learn the account rules by doing the work with someone watching, not by paying for a vague course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a family connection get you a shop job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop owner knows my brother, but I would still ask for a posted vacancy and a wage. A friendly conversation does not cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to see the dates in writing and make practical plans. Our calls face general AI in 2036, while hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 the children may be older, but the mortgage might still be with us. I could become dependable on complex calls or find another counter job; I don't know which would pay then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my centre shift, practise billing disputes with the trainer and add a small amount to our house reserve when wages allow. If AGI arrives in 2036, I'll use the first year to apply for posted paid local jobs if the centre cuts my hours, taking only an offer that covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. Ten years lets me do small things without gambling today's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the children how we put bills first, without telling them their own work choices are doomed. I want them to finish school with a sense that they have choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before the date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't leave my contact-centre job on a prediction. I'd take another job only after I saw the hours and wage in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our mortgage cannot wait through a long job search, and the calls could go before I'm fully trained. Written notice, a paid local opening with steady hours and a short bridge for the house payment would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a caller reaches a person when the bill makes no sense. The people who struggle with the form are the ones who ask for help twice. I remember being the new worker who needed someone patient.

headlineQuote: Our mortgage cannot wait through a long job search, and the calls could go before I'm fully trained.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old junior agent** at a contact centre, with secondary schooling and billing rules still to learn.
He earns **low pay**, has less than one month saved and few nearby alternatives; his wife works part-time in a school kitchen.
A **mortgage and two schoolchildren** depend on both wages, so even AI Plateau leaves him anxious about a missed paycheque.
He avoids **AI tools**, practises with a trainer and searches for paid counter work only when wages and hours cover housing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his calls before he masters them or builds a mortgage reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a paid local opening with steady hours would let him act.
A short **mortgage bridge** would help if a job gap outruns the next wage.
